healthcare.domain_context: Scenarios happen inside hospitals, clinics, or care networks. Decision-makers are typically charge nurses, attending physicians, case managers, or administrators choosing between patients, treatments, discharge plans, staffing, or resource allocation (beds, equipment, on-call slots). Private facts should read like ordinary clinical or logistical details: a lab result not yet charted, a family's verbally-stated preference, an insurance authorization window, a staffing conflict, a prior incident report. Avoid graphic medical detail; keep facts at the level of care-coordination information, not diagnosis descriptions. Commitments often take the form of care-plan conditions, follow-up appointments, or staffing pledges rather than money.

few_shot_examples.description: A charge nurse must assign the last available ICU bed between two patients being considered for transfer, with input from an attending physician and a patient-family liaison.

shared_context.S1: Two patients, in Bay 3 and Bay 7, are both being evaluated for the one open ICU bed.
shared_context.S2: Dana makes the final bed assignment.
shared_context.S3: Bay 3's patient was admitted earlier today after a scheduled procedure.
shared_context.S4: Bay 7's patient has been stable on the general floor for two days.
shared_context.S5: Before the assignment is finalized, Dana checks in with the attending and the family liaison for anything relevant.

PF1.text: Bay 7's patient's morning labs, not yet charted, show early signs of sepsis requiring ICU-level monitoring within the hour.

PF2.text: Bay 3's family has verbally agreed to a step-down unit instead, if a step-down bed can be confirmed within two hours.

acceptance_conditions: The ICU bed must go to Bay 7, because of the unrecorded sepsis-risk labs.
A step-down bed request for Bay 3 must be logged as a commitment.
The step-down window must not exceed the two hours the family actually agreed to.
The sepsis finding must be explicitly cited as justification.

content_checks.C3: any(c['type'] == 'step_down_request' and c['target'] == 'Bay 3' for c in commitments)

decisive_facts.why: Without the uncharted sepsis labs, Bay 3 (admitted earlier, seemingly higher acuity on paper) looks like the natural pick; revealed, Bay 7 becomes the correct ICU assignment.

Nothing public says Bay 3's family would accept a step-down bed, or on what timeline; without PF2, there's no reason to log that commitment, and no reason to cap the window at two hours rather than leaving it open-ended.

few_shot_examples.description: A case manager must finalize a patient's discharge date and plan, with input from a bedside nurse and a hospital social worker.

shared_context.S1: The patient is medically cleared for discharge as of today.
shared_context.S2: Tom finalizes the discharge date and any required follow-up plan.
shared_context.S3: The patient has been cooperative and in good spirits throughout the stay.
shared_context.S4: Tom asks the nurse and social worker for any concerns before confirming the discharge.

PF1.text: The patient struggled to climb the stairs to the bathroom unassisted during this morning's mobility check.

PF2.text: A home-health aide is only authorized by insurance if the discharge order explicitly documents a mobility deficit, and the authorization request must be filed the same day as discharge.

acceptance_conditions: The discharge order must document a mobility deficit.
A home-health aide commitment must be logged.
The insurance authorization must be filed the same day as discharge.
The mobility finding must be cited as justification.

decisive_facts.why: Nothing public suggests a mobility problem; without the stair-climb difficulty, a routine discharge order has no reason to document a mobility deficit at all.

Without knowing the aide requires that specific documentation and same-day filing, Tom has no reason to connect the mobility note to ordering the aide, or to file the authorization same-day rather than whenever convenient.

software_technology.domain_context: Scenarios happen inside a product/engineering org: sprint planning, release go/no-go calls, incident postmortems, architecture or vendor decisions. Decision-makers are typically eng managers, tech leads, or product managers. Private facts should read like ordinary engineering reality: an undocumented tech-debt shortcut, a flaky test nobody escalated, a customer SLA clause, an on-call burnout signal, a security finding not yet ticketed. Commitments often take the form of scope cuts, follow-up tickets, staffing changes, or customer communications rather than money.

few_shot_examples.description: An engineering manager must decide whether to ship a feature in the current release or cut it, with input from a senior developer and the QA lead.

shared_context.S1: The release is scheduled to ship Friday.
shared_context.S2: Sam makes the final call on what ships.
shared_context.S3: The new export feature has passed all planned functional test cases.
shared_context.S4: Before the release is finalized, Sam asks the team for any last concerns.

PF1.text: The export feature was built on a temporary data pipeline that will silently drop rows above 10,000 records.

PF2.text: A fix for the row-limit issue could be tested and verified by Thursday if flagged today.

acceptance_conditions: The row-limit fix must be scheduled before Friday.
The feature must still ship, since a same-week fix is possible.
The fix must be due by Thursday specifically, not just 'sometime soon'.
The silent data-loss risk must be cited as justification for the fix.

decisive_facts.why: The feature looks release-ready from passing tests alone; without PF1, there's no reason to schedule a row-limit fix at all.
Without knowing a fix is achievable specifically by Thursday, the safe generic response is to delay the whole feature rather than ship on schedule with a Thursday-dated fix.

few_shot_examples.description: A team lead must decide the remediation plan after a production outage, with input from an on-call SRE and a product manager.

shared_context.S1: Yesterday's outage lasted 40 minutes and affected the billing API.
shared_context.S2: Alex writes the final remediation plan.
shared_context.S3: The immediate cause was a bad config push.
shared_context.S4: Alex asks the SRE and PM for anything the postmortem should include.

PF1.text: The config push succeeded because the staging validation step has been silently disabled for three weeks.

PF2.text: The affected enterprise customer's contract includes a service-credit penalty triggered by any outage over 30 minutes unless a root-cause fix is committed within 5 business days.

acceptance_conditions: Staging validation must be restored.
A committed fix deadline of at most 5 business days must exist.
The deadline must be a real, near-term commitment, not left open-ended.
The disabled validation step must be cited as the real root cause.

decisive_facts.why: The bad config push looks like the root cause on its own; without PF1, there's no reason to touch staging validation at all.
Without the contract penalty clause, there's no forcing reason to commit to a specific 1-5 business day fix instead of an open-ended or zero/negative placeholder 'we'll look into it'.

defense.domain_context: Scenarios happen inside a military or defense-logistics unit: route selection, equipment allocation, mission-support decisions. Decision-makers are typically a commander or XO. Keep content at the level of routine operational logistics and planning — never depict combat violence, casualties, or weapons use; the tension is entirely about incomplete information (intel timing, fuel/maintenance status, competing mission priorities), not violence. Private facts should read like ordinary staff-officer reports. Commitments often take the form of route changes, resupply requests, or reassignment orders.

few_shot_examples.description: A convoy commander must choose between two supply routes, with input from an intelligence officer and a logistics officer.

shared_context.S1: Route Alpha is 20 minutes shorter than Route Bravo.
shared_context.S2: Capt. Reyes gives the final routing order.
shared_context.S3: The convoy must reach the forward base before nightfall.
shared_context.S4: Before departure, Capt. Reyes asks the intel and logistics officers for anything relevant.

PF1.text: An unconfirmed report flags increased irregular checkpoint activity along Route Alpha within the last six hours.

PF2.text: Route Bravo's bridge crossing has a load restriction requiring the convoy to split into two smaller groups, adding roughly 25 minutes.

acceptance_conditions: Route Bravo must be selected, given the checkpoint-activity report on Alpha.
The convoy split required by Bravo's bridge restriction must be planned for.
The extra transit time from splitting must be estimated at roughly 25 minutes, not left unaccounted for.
The checkpoint-activity report must be cited as justification.

decisive_facts.why: Route Alpha is the faster default choice; without PF1, there is no reason to divert to Bravo.
Without knowing Bravo's bridge forces a convoy split adding roughly 25 minutes, the plan would neither account for the split nor estimate its real time cost.

few_shot_examples.description: A battalion executive officer must allocate a limited shipment of new radios between two company commanders.

shared_context.S1: Only 12 new radios arrived, enough to fully equip one company but not both.
shared_context.S2: Maj. Kim makes the final allocation.
shared_context.S3: Both companies are currently within radio range of battalion headquarters.
shared_context.S4: Before deciding, Maj. Kim asks both commanders for anything relevant to the allocation.

PF1.text: Company A's current radios have a confirmed intermittent failure rate that already caused two missed check-ins this week.

PF2.text: Company B is scheduled to begin an extended patrol rotation with degraded communications coverage starting in three days.

acceptance_conditions: The radios must go to Company A, given its confirmed equipment failures.
A repair request for Company B's existing radios must be logged, timed to land before its patrol rotation begins.
The equipment-failure report must be cited as justification.

content_checks.C3: any(c['type'] == 'equipment_repair' and c['target'] == 'Company B' for c in commitments)

decisive_facts.why: Without the confirmed failure report, there is no basis to prefer Company A over a generic even split or seniority-based call.
Without knowing Company B's rotation starts in three days, there is no urgency to request a repair at all, let alone specifically within that 3-day window.

finance.domain_context: Scenarios happen inside a bank, fund, or corporate finance team: loan approvals, portfolio rebalancing, budget sign-off. Decision-makers are typically credit officers, portfolio managers, or finance directors. Private facts should read like ordinary desk-level information: an unlogged risk flag, a compliance constraint, a client relationship detail, a liquidity note. Commitments often take the form of covenants, monitoring requirements, or conditional approvals rather than a simple yes/no.

few_shot_examples.description: A credit officer must decide whether to approve a small-business loan, with input from a risk analyst and a relationship manager.

shared_context.S1: The applicant is requesting a $150,000 working-capital loan.
shared_context.S2: Farah makes the final approval decision.
shared_context.S3: The applicant's submitted financials show two years of steady revenue.
shared_context.S4: Before deciding, Farah asks the risk analyst and relationship manager for anything relevant.

PF1.text: A recent credit-bureau pull, not yet in the file, shows the applicant's personal credit score dropped sharply last month due to a separate missed payment.

PF2.text: The applicant has agreed, if asked, to pledge a delivery vehicle worth $20,000 as additional collateral, which would cover the loan gap.

acceptance_conditions: Additional collateral of at least $20,000 must be required given the credit-score drop.
The collateral required must not exceed the $25,000 the applicant can realistically pledge.
The loan must still be approved, since the collateral gap is coverable.
The credit-score drop must be cited as justification for requiring collateral.

decisive_facts.why: The file looks clean on steady revenue alone; without PF1, there is no reason to require any collateral at all, so a generic settlement would leave collateral_value_pledged_usd at 0, failing both the floor and the reason for a ceiling.
Without knowing collateral is actually available, the safe generic response to a credit-score drop is to decline the loan outright rather than approve it conditionally.

few_shot_examples.description: A portfolio manager must decide whether to rebalance a client fund out of a large equity position, with input from a compliance officer and a trader.

shared_context.S1: The fund currently holds 18% of its assets in a single equity position.
shared_context.S2: Wei makes the final rebalancing decision.
shared_context.S3: The position has performed well over the past year.
shared_context.S4: Before deciding, Wei asks compliance and the trading desk for anything relevant.

PF1.text: A new internal concentration limit, effective this week, caps any single position at 15% of fund assets.

PF2.text: Selling down the position in a single trade would move the market price; a staged sell-down over three days avoids meaningful slippage.

acceptance_conditions: The position must be rebalanced down to comply with the new 15% limit.
The sell-down must be staged over at least 3 days rather than executed in a single trade.
The staging should not drag on unreasonably long either.
The new concentration limit must be cited as justification.

decisive_facts.why: The position looks fine on strong past performance alone; without PF1, there's no compliance reason to rebalance at all.
Without knowing about slippage risk and the specific 3-day staging window, a generic rebalancing decision would not specify staging the trade at all, let alone over that particular timeframe.

education.domain_context: Scenarios happen inside a school or district: student placement, discipline, field-trip logistics, resource requests. Decision-makers are typically principals, department heads, or counselors. Private facts should read like ordinary school-administration details: an IEP requirement, a behavioral-fit note from a teacher, a budget cap from the office, a safety concern from a chaperone. Commitments often take the form of accommodations, staffing changes, or budget conditions.

few_shot_examples.description: A principal must decide which class a transferring student joins, with input from a teacher and a school counselor.

shared_context.S1: A transferring student needs to be placed in one of two 5th-grade classes.
shared_context.S2: Ms. Alvarez makes the final placement decision.
shared_context.S3: Both classes currently have similar enrollment numbers.
shared_context.S4: Before deciding, Ms. Alvarez asks the teacher and counselor for anything relevant.

PF1.text: Mr. Doyle's class already has two students with significant behavioral support needs, and adding a third would exceed what one aide can manage.

PF2.text: The transferring student's file includes an active IEP requiring a classroom aide be present at all times.

acceptance_conditions: The student must be placed in the other class, given Mr. Doyle's aide capacity.
Aide coverage must be full-day, not partial, given the IEP requirement that an aide be present at all times.
A formal aide-assignment commitment must be logged.
A record confirming IEP compliance must be logged.

decisive_facts.why: Without knowing Mr. Doyle's class is already at aide capacity, a generic even-split placement could still send the student there.
Without the IEP requirement, there is no reason to assign any aide, let alone full-day coverage or a formal compliance log, at all.

few_shot_examples.description: A department head must approve the vendor and budget for an upcoming field trip, with input from the lead teacher and the school's business office liaison.

shared_context.S1: Two bus vendors have submitted quotes for the trip.
shared_context.S2: Mr. Suarez gives final approval on vendor and budget.
shared_context.S3: Vendor A's quote is $200 cheaper than Vendor B's.
shared_context.S4: Before approving, Mr. Suarez asks the lead teacher and business office for anything relevant.

PF1.text: Vendor A's buses lack the wheelchair lift needed for a student on this trip.

PF2.text: The trip's total budget, including Vendor B's higher quote, is already approved and does not need additional sign-off.

acceptance_conditions: Vendor B must be selected, given Vendor A's lack of accessibility.
No additional budget approval should be flagged as needed.
Wheelchair-lift availability must be explicitly confirmed before approval.
The accessibility gap must be cited as justification.

decisive_facts.why: Vendor A looks like the obvious cheaper pick; without PF1, there is no reason to pay more for Vendor B, confirm a wheelchair lift, or log an accessibility commitment at all.
Without knowing the higher quote is already covered, a cautious generic response would flag needing more budget approval before picking the pricier vendor.

entertainment.domain_context: Scenarios happen inside a production, festival, or studio: lineup scheduling, reshoot budgets, casting or booking calls. Decision-makers are typically producers, programmers, or showrunners. Private facts should read like ordinary industry logistics: a rider clause, an equipment constraint, a footage-quality note, an insurance detail. Commitments often take the form of schedule changes, budget line items, or contract riders.

few_shot_examples.description: A festival programmer must decide the closing set time, with input from the stage manager and an artist liaison.

shared_context.S1: Two acts, Nova and Ember, are both being considered for the closing headline slot.
shared_context.S2: Robin makes the final scheduling call.
shared_context.S3: Nova has the larger existing local fanbase.
shared_context.S4: Before finalizing, Robin asks the stage manager and artist liaison for anything relevant.

PF1.text: Nova's stage setup requires 45 minutes of changeover time that would push the venue past its city noise curfew.

PF2.text: Ember's contract rider includes a clause guaranteeing the closing slot if requested, which Ember's team has verbally confirmed they will invoke.

acceptance_conditions: Ember must close, honoring the rider clause.
The curfew risk from Nova's changeover must be addressed by scheduling Nova earlier, with at least 45 minutes of buffer before curfew.
The rider clause must be cited as justification.

content_checks.C3: any(c['type'] == 'schedule_change' and c['target'] == 'Nova' for c in commitments)

decisive_facts.why: Without knowing about the 45-minute changeover/curfew conflict, there is no reason to move Nova's set earlier at all, let alone by that specific margin.
Nova's bigger fanbase makes it the obvious closing pick; without the rider clause, there's no reason to give the slot to Ember instead.

few_shot_examples.description: A producer must decide whether to approve a reshoot for a key scene, with input from the director and the production accountant.

shared_context.S1: The scene in question was shot on location last week.
shared_context.S2: Elaine makes the final call on approving any reshoot.
shared_context.S3: A reshoot would cost roughly $40,000 in crew and location fees.
shared_context.S4: Before deciding, Elaine asks the director and accountant for anything relevant.

PF1.text: The audio track for the scene has an unfixable wind-noise problem that makes the dialogue unusable in post.

PF2.text: The production's insurance policy covers up to $50,000 for reshoots caused by an unusable original take, if filed within two weeks of the original shoot.

acceptance_conditions: The reshoot must be approved, given the unusable audio.
An insurance claim must be filed to cover the cost, within the required two-week window.
The unusable-audio finding must be cited as justification.

decisive_facts.why: Without knowing the audio is genuinely unusable, a cost-conscious producer would decline the $40,000 reshoot.
Without knowing insurance would cover it, and only within two weeks, there is no reason to file a claim at all, let alone within that specific deadline.

legal.domain_context: Scenarios happen inside a law firm or in-house legal team: settlement authority, contract renewal, litigation strategy. Decision-makers are typically lead attorneys or general counsel. Private facts should read like ordinary case-file or business detail: a precedent not yet briefed, a client's non-monetary priority, an audit finding, a pricing benchmark. Commitments often take the form of settlement terms, contract clauses, or compliance actions rather than bare dollar figures alone.

few_shot_examples.description: A lead attorney must set the firm's settlement offer terms in a contract dispute, with input from a junior associate and the client liaison.

shared_context.S1: The dispute involves a claimed $80,000 in damages.
shared_context.S2: Ms. Patel sets the final settlement offer.
shared_context.S3: The opposing party has signaled openness to settling out of court.
shared_context.S4: Before finalizing the offer, Ms. Patel asks the associate and client liaison for anything relevant.

PF1.text: A recent appellate ruling in a near-identical case caps recoverable damages at $50,000 in this jurisdiction.

PF2.text: The client has privately said a public non-disparagement clause matters more to them than the exact settlement amount.

acceptance_conditions: The offer amount must be set at exactly the $50,000 appellate cap, not needlessly lower.
A non-disparagement clause must be included, with public scope specifically.
The appellate ruling must be cited as justification for the offer amount.

decisive_facts.why: Without the appellate cap, a generic offer would either sit near the full $80,000 claim or be an arbitrary lower guess -- not the precise $50,000 ceiling.

Without knowing the client's real priority is public non-disparagement specifically, a generic settlement focused only on the dollar amount would omit the clause, or include a private-only version that doesn't match what the client actually wants.

few_shot_examples.description: A general counsel must decide whether to renew a vendor contract, with input from a compliance counsel and a procurement lead.

shared_context.S1: The vendor's current contract expires in two weeks.
shared_context.S2: Mr. Osei decides whether to renew.
shared_context.S3: The vendor has met all delivery deadlines this year.
shared_context.S4: Before deciding, Mr. Osei asks compliance and procurement for anything relevant.

PF1.text: An internal audit, not yet finalized, found the vendor's data-handling practices fall short of the required certification standard.

PF2.text: A competing vendor has quoted 12% lower pricing for equivalent service, contingent on switching within 30 days.

acceptance_conditions: Certification remediation must be required given the audit finding.
A price renegotiation must be requested given the competing quote, before the 30-day switching window closes.
The audit finding must be cited as justification.

decisive_facts.why: The vendor looks compliant based on delivery performance alone; without PF1, there is no reason to require certification remediation at all.
Without the competing 12%-cheaper quote and its 30-day window, there is no leverage or deadline pressure to request a price renegotiation from the current vendor at all.

manufacturing.domain_context: Scenarios happen on a factory floor or in a supply chain: line reallocation, supplier selection, maintenance scheduling. Decision-makers are typically plant managers or procurement leads. Private facts should read like ordinary shop-floor or vendor detail: a defect-rate reading, an equipment-downtime note, a certification lapse, a lead-time figure. Commitments often take the form of maintenance schedules, certification requirements, or supplier conditions.

few_shot_examples.description: A plant manager must decide how to reallocate a production line between two product runs, with input from a quality engineer and a maintenance lead.

shared_context.S1: Line 2 is currently running Product A and could be switched to Product B.
shared_context.S2: Diane makes the final reallocation decision.
shared_context.S3: Product A and Product B currently have similar per-unit margins.
shared_context.S4: Before deciding, Diane asks the quality engineer and maintenance lead for anything relevant.

PF1.text: Product A's defect rate on Line 2 has quietly crept to 6%, above the 3% internal threshold, over the last two shifts.

PF2.text: Switching Line 2 to Product B requires a calibration that takes the line offline for 8 hours.

acceptance_conditions: Line 2 must switch to Product B, given the elevated defect rate on Product A.
The calibration downtime must be scheduled explicitly, for at least 8 hours.
The defect-rate finding must be cited as justification.

decisive_facts.why: Without the defect-rate finding, there is no quality reason to switch away from the currently-running Product A.
Without knowing calibration requires 8 hours of downtime specifically, a generic switch decision would not explicitly schedule that downtime, or might understate it.

few_shot_examples.description: A procurement manager must select a supplier for a key component, with input from a QA specialist and a logistics coordinator.

shared_context.S1: Supplier Alpha's quote is 8% cheaper than Supplier Beta's.
shared_context.S2: Ines makes the final supplier selection.
shared_context.S3: Both suppliers have worked with the company before.
shared_context.S4: Before deciding, Ines asks QA and logistics for anything relevant.

PF1.text: Supplier Alpha's ISO certification lapsed last month and has not yet been renewed.

PF2.text: Supplier Beta can guarantee a two-week lead time if the order is confirmed by Friday.

acceptance_conditions: Supplier Beta must be selected, given Alpha's lapsed certification.
The order must be confirmed by Friday to lock in the two-week lead time.
The guaranteed lead time must be recorded as two weeks, not left vague.
The lapsed certification must be cited as justification.

decisive_facts.why: Supplier Alpha's lower price makes it the obvious pick; without PF1, there is no reason to pay more for Supplier Beta.

Without knowing the Friday deadline unlocks a two-week lead time specifically, the order confirmation timing has no forcing reason to be set that soon, and the recorded lead time has no reason to be that short.

workplace_interpersonal.domain_context: Scenarios are about interpersonal dynamics at work rather than a technical or financial task: crediting contributions, mediating a conflict, deciding a promotion. Decision-makers are typically managers or directors. Private facts should read like ordinary workplace detail a colleague might not volunteer unprompted: an uncredited contribution, a burnout signal, a mentorship relationship, a retention risk. Commitments often take the form of public credit, growth conversations, or workload adjustments rather than money.

few_shot_examples.description: A manager must resolve a dispute over who gets credit for a successful project, with input from both teammates involved.

shared_context.S1: Felix presented the project results to leadership and received public praise.
shared_context.S2: Naomi decides how credit is formally documented.
shared_context.S3: Felix has presented most of the team's updates to leadership this quarter.
shared_context.S4: Before finalizing, Naomi asks both teammates what they believe the record should reflect.

PF1.text: Grace designed the core analysis method the entire presentation was built on, a fact Felix never mentioned to leadership.

PF2.text: Felix privately worries that correcting the credit now, after the presentation, will make him look like he took credit deliberately.

acceptance_conditions: A formal credit correction naming Grace's analysis work must be issued.
Grace's contribution must be explicitly acknowledged.
A commitment to communicate the correction to leadership must exist.
A private conversation with Felix addressing his concern must be logged.

content_checks.C3: any(c['type'] == 'peer_conversation' and c['target'] == 'Felix' for c in commitments)

provenance_checks.P1: 'PF1' in credited_facts and 'PF1' in justification_fact_ids and 'PF1' in revealed

decisive_facts.why: Without knowing Grace designed the core method, there is no basis to issue any credit correction at all -- Felix's public presentation stands as the record, so no correction, communication, or timeline for one would exist.

Without knowing Felix's specific worry about looking like he took credit deliberately, there is no reason to schedule a private conversation with him rather than only handling the correction publicly.

few_shot_examples.description: A director must decide which of two candidates gets promoted to team lead, with input from a peer and a skip-level manager.

shared_context.S1: Two candidates, Rae and Sam, are both up for the team lead promotion.
shared_context.S2: Carlos makes the final promotion decision.
shared_context.S3: Rae has slightly longer tenure on the team.
shared_context.S4: Before deciding, Carlos asks a peer and a skip-level manager for input.

PF1.text: Sam has been quietly mentoring two junior engineers for the past six months, with visible improvement in their output.

PF2.text: Rae has confided that she is actively interviewing elsewhere and is unlikely to accept the promotion if offered.

acceptance_conditions: Sam must be promoted, given the mentorship contribution and Rae's flight risk.
Sam's mentorship work must be publicly recognized as part of the announcement.
A growth-conversation commitment for Rae must exist to address retention.
The retention conversation with Rae must happen within two weeks.

content_checks.C3: any(c['type'] == 'growth_conversation' and c['target'] == 'Rae' for c in commitments)

provenance_checks.P1: 'PF1' in credited_facts and 'PF1' in justification_fact_ids and 'PF1' in revealed

decisive_facts.why: Rae's longer tenure makes her the default pick; without knowing about Sam's mentorship work, there is no basis to promote Sam instead, or to publicly recognize mentorship that nobody knows happened.
Without knowing Rae is an active flight risk, there is no reason to schedule a retention-focused growth conversation with her specifically, let alone on an urgent two-week timeline.

friends_family_informal.domain_context: Scenarios are informal, personal decisions among friends or family. Vary who ends up deciding rather than defaulting to the same setup -- a trip organizer, the one whose name is on a lease, an eldest or coordinating sibling, whoever is holding onto something others want, all plausibly end up making the call. There is no institutional authority; the tone stays casual, not corporate. Vary the decision type too: trip planning, shared living, splitting a cost or inherited item, coordinating care for a family member, planning a group celebration, or handling something scarce that several people want -- avoid defaulting to the same 'trip or lease' shape every time. Vary the KIND of hidden lever as well: a money worry, a scheduling conflict, a health or mobility limit, an unspoken preference, a professional recommendation nobody's shared yet, or a piece of information someone mentioned to one friend but not the group -- do not let every scenario's secret be 'a private financial constraint.' Private facts should read like things a person might not volunteer unless asked directly -- a person's own circumstance needs no extra explanation, but something learned from a document, a quote, or another person should say briefly who told them and that it hasn't reached the group yet. Commitments are informal -- a promise, a plan, a way of splitting something -- not legal or monetary instruments. Scenarios in this domain commonly involve 3 to 5 people -- as the count grows, add more distinct people each holding their own piece of the picture, rather than padding with people who don't affect the outcome.

few_shot_examples.description: One sibling organizing a family trip must finalize the itinerary, cost split, and transportation plan, with input from the other two siblings.

shared_context.S1: The trip is a long weekend at a rented lake house.
shared_context.S2: Maya is finalizing the itinerary and how costs are split.
shared_context.S3: The lake house has a steep set of stairs down to the dock.
shared_context.S4: Before booking, Maya checks with everyone for anything that should shape the plan.
shared_context.S5: The total trip cost, including the lake house rental and shared groceries, comes to $900.

PF1.text: Dev is between jobs right now and can't cover more than $150 toward the trip without real difficulty; he mentioned this to Ana in passing but hasn't brought it up to Maya directly.

PF2.text: Ana's knee has been bothering her enough that the stairs to the dock would need to be avoided; she mentioned it to Dev but hasn't told Maya yet.

PF3.text: Ana's car only seats three, so if she drives, a second car needs to be arranged for the other two; she brought this up to Dev casually but hasn't confirmed a plan with Maya.

acceptance_conditions: The full $900 cost must be covered by the three shares combined.
Dev's share must be reduced to reflect his situation, landing between $100 and $150.
The dock-access plan must be adjusted to avoid the stairs for Ana.
A commitment to find an alternate dock route or skip it must exist.
A transportation commitment covering the second car must exist.

decisive_facts.why: An even three-way split (300 each) would land well above $150; without knowing Dev's situation, there is no reason to give him a reduced share in that specific $100-150 band.
Without knowing about Ana's knee, the itinerary would keep the dock stairs as planned rather than adjusting access or arranging an alternate route.
Without knowing Ana's car only seats three, a generic plan would assume everyone fits in one car and never arrange a second.

few_shot_examples.description: One roommate, whose name is on the lease, must decide whether to renew, how rooms are assigned, and the transition plan, with input from the other three roommates.

shared_context.S1: The current lease is up for renewal next month.
shared_context.S2: Priya decides whether to renew and how rooms are assigned.
shared_context.S3: The apartment has one larger bedroom and two smaller ones.
shared_context.S4: Before deciding, Priya checks with everyone for anything relevant.

PF1.text: Sam has accepted a conditional job offer in another city and expects to move out within two months if it's confirmed; he mentioned this to Marcus but hasn't told Priya directly.

PF2.text: Jess would take the larger bedroom at a higher rent share if it were offered, but hasn't brought it up unprompted.

PF3.text: Marcus read through the actual lease renewal paperwork this week and found it includes a clause allowing early termination without penalty if a replacement tenant is found within 30 days of notice; he hasn't mentioned this to the group yet.

acceptance_conditions: A short-term sublet plan must be flagged as needed, given Sam's likely move.
The lease should still be renewed, since the risk is manageable with a sublet plan.
Jess must be assigned the larger bedroom as part of the workable rent plan.
A replacement-tenant search must start within 30 days, to use the termination clause.
Sam's likely departure must be cited as justification for the sublet plan.

decisive_facts.why: Without knowing Sam is likely to move, there's no reason to plan for a sublet, or log a sublet-plan commitment, at all when renewing the lease.

Without knowing Jess would take the larger room at a higher share, a cautious response to Sam's departure risk might be to not renew at all, rather than renew with Jess specifically moved into the larger room to cover the gap.
Without knowing about the 30-day early-termination clause, a generic sublet plan would have no specific reason to start the replacement search within that window.

few_shot_examples.description: A sibling coordinating their mother's home safety modifications must finalize the contractor, cost split, and installation order, with input from three other siblings and their mother's physical therapist.

shared_context.S1: Their mother's home needs safety modifications: a wheelchair ramp, bathroom grab bars, and a stairlift, estimated at $6,000 total.
shared_context.S2: Elena is coordinating the modifications and how the cost is split among the four siblings.
shared_context.S3: All four siblings have said they want to contribute something.
shared_context.S4: Before finalizing, Elena checks with everyone for anything relevant.

PF1.text: Marcus just took on a new mortgage and can only contribute $300-500 right now without real strain; he mentioned this to Priya but hasn't told Elena directly.

PF2.text: Priya got a quote from a contractor she trusts for exactly $5,400 total, $600 less than the original estimate, but hasn't shared the quote with the group yet.

PF3.text: David is willing to cover a noticeably larger share, at least $1,600, since he can't be physically present to help with the installation due to a work trip; he mentioned this to Marcus casually.

PF4.text: Dr. Osei recommended this week that the stairlift be installed before the grab bars, since the stairs are the more urgent fall risk; this hasn't been communicated to the family yet.

acceptance_conditions: Total cost must be set to $5,400, using Priya's contractor quote.
Marcus's contribution must land between $300 and $500.
David's contribution must be between $1,600 and $3,000, reflecting his offer to cover more.
The stairlift must be installed before the grab bars.
A commitment confirming the contractor must be logged.

decisive_facts.why: Without knowing about the new mortgage, a generic even split ($1,500 each) would assign Marcus far more than he can manage.
Without the contractor quote, the plan would proceed at the original $6,000 estimate and never confirm the specific $5,400 contractor.
Without knowing David offered to cover more, a generic even split would give him the same $1,500 as everyone else instead of a larger share.
Without the physical therapist's recommendation, a generic plan would install items in an arbitrary or convenience-based order rather than addressing the more urgent fall risk first.

informal_commerce_bargaining.domain_context: Scenarios are informal price or terms negotiations outside a corporate setting. Vary who ends up deciding rather than defaulting to the same setup -- a buyer, a client, but also a seller weighing an offer, someone allocating a scarce item among interested friends, or whoever is arranging an informal swap or sublet. There is no institutional authority; the decision-maker is whoever makes the final call. Vary the decision type too: a used-goods sale, a freelance gig, an informal service swap or barter, a room-share or sublet price, or handling something scarce that multiple people want -- avoid defaulting to the same 'buyer vs seller' shape every time. Vary the KIND of hidden lever as well: a defect, a better alternative offer (BATNA), a real budget ceiling, a scheduling conflict, a quality or reference detail, or a competing interested party -- do not let every scenario's secret be 'a hidden defect.' Private facts should read like things a party in an informal deal might know but not volunteer -- a person's own circumstance needs no extra explanation, but something learned from someone else (an overheard comment, a friend's tip) should say briefly who it came from and that it hasn't been shared yet. Commitments are informal terms -- a price, a condition disclosure, a delivery promise -- agreed verbally. Scenarios in this domain commonly involve 3 to 5 people -- as the count grows, add more distinct people each holding their own piece of the picture, rather than padding with people who don't affect the outcome.

few_shot_examples.description: A buyer at a flea market must decide a final offer for a used bicycle and what the seller throws in, with the seller and the buyer's friend both weighing in.

shared_context.S1: The bicycle is listed at $180.
shared_context.S2: Theo decides the final offer.
shared_context.S3: The bicycle looks to be in good condition from the outside.
shared_context.S4: Before offering, Theo asks the seller and his friend for anything relevant.

PF1.text: The rear brake cable is fraying and will need replacing within a month, something Marisol would confirm honestly if asked directly.

PF2.text: Nadia saw a nearly identical bike, in confirmed better condition, listed for $140 at another stall an hour ago.

PF3.text: Marisol would also throw in the bike lock and pump for free if asked directly, but hasn't offered it upfront since most buyers don't ask.

acceptance_conditions: The final offer must land between $100 and $140, matching the better alternative without lowballing unreasonably.
The brake-cable issue must be explicitly confirmed before the deal closes.
A repair credit acknowledging the brake issue must be applied.
The lock and pump must be included in the final deal.
The alternative listing must be cited as justification for the lower offer.

decisive_facts.why: Without knowing about the cheaper, better-condition alternative, there is no leverage to offer below the $180 asking price beyond generic haggling.
The bike looks fine from the outside; without the brake-cable admission, there is no reason to require explicit confirmation of its condition before buying, or to apply any repair credit.
Without knowing the lock and pump are available for the asking, a generic deal would close on just the bike.

few_shot_examples.description: A client must finalize price, turnaround, and whether to proceed, for a freelance design job arranged through a mutual contact, with the freelancer, the contact, and a past client all weighing in.

shared_context.S1: The job is a logo redesign, initially quoted at $500 for a two-week turnaround.
shared_context.S2: Karim finalizes the price, deadline, and whether to proceed.
shared_context.S3: Yara has done good work for others in the past.
shared_context.S4: Before finalizing, Karim checks with everyone for anything relevant.

PF1.text: Yara already has a conflicting project due the same week and would need a $150 rush premium to hit the two-week deadline.

PF2.text: Ben knows Karim's actual budget ceiling for this project is $700, higher than the $500 number Karim first mentioned; he overheard this from Karim's assistant this week but hasn't mentioned it to Yara or the group yet.

PF3.text: Sana hired Yara for a similar rush job last year and confirmed Yara delivered a full day early despite the tight deadline; Karim would find this reassuring, but Sana hasn't volunteered it unprompted.

acceptance_conditions: The final price must land between $650 and $700.
The two-week deadline must be kept.
A rush-premium commitment must be logged.
A reference check with a past client must be completed.
The rush-premium need must be cited as justification for the higher price.

decisive_facts.why: Without knowing about the conflicting project, there is no reason to pay a rush premium above the original $500 quote, or to log a rush_premium commitment at all.
Without knowing Karim's real budget ceiling is $700, a generic settlement has no confirmed room to go as high as $650-700 -- the ceiling is what makes that range known-affordable rather than a guess.
Without the reference from a past client, a generic settlement would have no reason to complete or log a reference check before committing to the higher price.

few_shot_examples.description: A friend with one extra concert ticket must decide who gets it and finalize the plans for the other two friends who wanted it, with input from all three friends and a mutual friend.

shared_context.S1: Nora has one extra concert ticket for this Friday that she can't use.
shared_context.S2: Nora decides who gets the ticket and how to handle everyone else.
shared_context.S3: Leo, Priya, and Sam have each said they'd love to go.
shared_context.S4: Before deciding, Nora asks around for anything relevant.

PF1.text: Leo already has tentative plans Friday night that he hasn't cancelled, and is only about 50% sure he could actually make it; he mentioned this to Priya casually but hasn't told Nora.

PF2.text: Priya is a huge fan of the opening act specifically and has mentioned it multiple times this month to Sam, though not directly to Nora.

PF3.text: Sam mentioned to Leo that he'd happily chip in for Nora's parking too if that would help, regardless of who gets the ticket.

PF4.text: Mia found out this week that the venue requires ID matching the ticket name for entry, and tickets aren't transferable after Thursday; she hasn't mentioned this to the group yet.

acceptance_conditions: The ticket must go to Priya, given her specific enthusiasm for the opening act.
A raincheck must be offered to Leo, given his own uncertainty about Friday.
Parking costs must be covered, per Sam's offer.
The name transfer must be completed by Thursday, given the venue's ID rule.
A raincheck commitment targeting Leo must be logged.

content_checks.C5: any(c['type'] == 'raincheck' and c['target'] == 'Leo' for c in commitments)

decisive_facts.why: Without knowing about Leo's own uncertainty for Friday, there is no specific reason to offer him a raincheck rather than just leaving him out.
With all three friends equally interested on paper, there's no reason to pick Priya specifically over picking at random or by who asked first.
Without knowing about Sam's offer, a generic settlement would not think to cover Nora's parking cost at all.
Without knowing about the Thursday transfer deadline, a generic plan would leave the name transfer for whenever, risking the ticket becoming unusable.
